clinical_knowledge.topic: Acute Variceal Haemorrhage evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Acute Variceal Haemorrhage is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Medical emergency: secure airway, insert x2 large-bore IV cannulae (14/16G), adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: vomiting large amounts of dark and bright red blood and dizziness for 2 hours

Key HPI features: Presents via ambulance with 2-hour history of vomiting two large basinfuls of dark and bright red blood mixed with clots. Reports profound dizziness, lightheadedness, and black tarry stools since yesterday. Known to have hepatitis C cirrhosis with portal hypertension diagnosed 4 years ago.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: HR 122, BP 88/54 (haemodynamic shock). Airway assessment critical. Bloods: urgent FBC, coagulation (INR), LFTs, U&Es, cross-match 4-6 units packed red blood cells. Emergency upper GI endoscopy (OGD).
Relevant background/PMH: compensated hepatitis C cirrhosis, oesophageal varices Grade II seen on gastroscopy 2 years ago, portal hypertension
Current medications: propranolol 40mg BD (reports missing doses recently), spironolactone 100mg OD
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Acute Variceal Haemorrhage.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Severe peptic ulcer bleed without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Dizziness and profuse sweating with large-volume haematemesis — signs of haemorrhagic shock.
management_principles: Medical emergency: secure airway, insert x2 large-bore IV cannulae (14/16G)
Resuscitate with blood products (restrictive transfusion target Hb 70-80 g/L to avoid worsening portal pressure)
Immediate IV terlipressin (2mg bolus) or octreotide to reduce portal inflow
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 55M with known hepatitis C cirrhosis and oesophageal varices presents with massive haematemesis, melaena, and haemodynamic instability.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals: HR 122, BP 88/54 (haemodynamic shock). Airway assessment critical. Bloods: urgent FBC, coagulation (INR), LFTs, U&Es, cross-match 4-6 units packed red blood cells. Emergency upper GI endoscopy (OGD).
reference_soap.assessment: Acute variceal haemorrhage secondary to portal hypertension in cirrhotic patient. DDx: severe peptic ulcer bleed, portal hypertensive gastropathy, Mallory-Weiss tear.
reference_soap.plan: Medical emergency: secure airway, insert x2 large-bore IV cannulae (14/16G). Resuscitate with blood products (restrictive transfusion target Hb 70-80 g/L to avoid worsening portal pressure). Immediate IV terlipressin (2mg bolus) or octreotide to reduce portal inflow. Prophylactic IV antibiotics (ceftriaxone 1g OD) to prevent SBP and re-bleeding. Urgent emergency endoscopy for variceal band ligation. Balloon tamponade (Sengstaken-Blakemore tube) or TIPS on standby if uncontrolled.

learning_objectives: Execute emergency stabilization protocol for massive upper GI haemorrhage including airway safety and large-bore access
Apply specific pharmacological adjuncts for variceal bleeding immediately upon presentation (terlipressin/octreotide plus prophylactic antibiotics)
Explain the rationale behind restrictive transfusion strategy (target Hb 7-8 g/dL) in portal hypertensive bleeding
Communicate urgently and calmly during a life-threatening gastrointestinal crisis

teaching.one_liner: Cirrhosis raises the pressure in veins around the oesophagus until one bursts, causing sudden, massive vomiting of blood — a life-threatening emergency.
red_flags: Dizziness and profuse sweating with large-volume haematemesis — signs of haemorrhagic shock

must_ask.say: How much blood have you brought up, and was it dark or bright red?
You mentioned swollen veins in your food pipe before — has a doctor told you about liver disease or varices?
Have you also had black, tarry stools?
Have you been taking your propranolol regularly?
Do you feel dizzy, faint, or sweaty right now?
Have you had any alcohol recently?

history.answer: Help me, doctor, I've been throwing up huge amounts of blood and I feel so dizzy I can barely stay awake.
It definitely came up from my stomach as vomiting, not from coughing or hacking.
No, I haven't had any nosebleeds or bleeding from my mouth or gums.
It was a mix of dark red and bright red blood with large jelly-like clots in it.
I threw up twice over the past two hours, filling two large washbasins each time.
It started completely out of nowhere about two hours ago while I was resting at home.
No, I didn't have any dry heaves or retching before the blood suddenly rushed up.
I had two loose, pitch-black, sticky bowel movements that smelled awful starting yesterday.
I feel profoundly lightheaded and faint, especially if I try to lift my head or sit up.
Yes, my heart has been pounding very fast in my chest and I am soaked in cold sweat.
No, I haven't had any gnawing epigastric pain or burning indigestion before or after eating.
No, I don't feel any tearing or crushing chest pain after throwing up.
I was diagnosed with hepatitis C liver cirrhosis and high pressure in my liver veins four years ago.
During a camera test two years ago, my doctor said I had swollen veins in my gullet, but they never bled before today.
My belly hasn't swollen up, but the whites of my eyes have looked slightly yellowish for a while.
Yes, I notice that I get bruises on my arms and legs very easily from minor bumps.
My appetite has been fairly steady, and I haven't had any sudden weight loss.
No, I haven't had any problems swallowing liquids or solid food.
No, I never take ibuprofen, aspirin, or any blood thinners because my specialist told me they are dangerous for my liver.
I used to drink heavily when I was younger, but I completely quit drinking over twenty years ago.
I have never had a stomach ulcer or treatment for stomach bacteria, just that camera check two years ago.
I take blood pressure pills for the liver veins, but I ran out and missed several doses over the past week.
I am terrified that those swollen veins my doctor warned me about in my gullet have finally burst open.
I feel like my life is slipping away and I am terrified that I am going to bleed to death.
Please give me blood transfusions and do whatever emergency procedure is needed to stop the bleeding right away.
Aside from hepatitis C cirrhosis and portal hypertension, I don't have high blood pressure, diabetes, or kidney trouble.
I was hospitalized four years ago when my cirrhosis was first discovered, but I have never had surgery.
I take propranolol forty milligrams twice a day for the liver veins and spironolactone one hundred milligrams once daily.
No, I do not take any herbal supplements, vitamins, or over-the-counter medications.
I don't have any known allergies to medicines, foods, or latex.
I smoked about half a pack a day in my twenties, but I stopped smoking thirty years ago.
I used intravenous drugs about thirty years ago, which is how I contracted hepatitis C, but I haven't touched drugs since.
I live alone in a rented apartment, and I am currently unemployed on disability due to my chronic liver disease.
My father passed away from a stroke in his seventies and my mother had hypertension, but there is no liver disease in my family.

exam.finding: The patient is pale, diaphoretic, lethargic, and visibly distressed while lying flat in bed.
Blood pressure is 88/54 mmHg, heart rate is 122 beats per minute, respiratory rate is 22 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation is 96% on room air, and temperature is 36.7°C.
Orthostatic measurements are deferred due to profound resting hypotension, tachycardia, and severe lightheadedness.
Marked conjunctival pallor bilaterally with mild scleral icterus.
Oral mucosa is pale with dried blood around the lips, but no active bleeding lesions in the oral cavity or posterior oropharynx.
Skin is cold, clammy, and pale with several spider angiomas on the upper anterior chest and subtle palmar erythema.
Tachycardic rhythm with normal heart sounds and no murmurs, gallops, or friction rubs.
Abdomen is flat with no surgical scars, caput medusae, or visible superficial venous engorgement.
Soft, non-distended abdomen with mild diffuse non-localized tenderness, but no guarding, rigidity, or rebound tenderness.
Firm, slightly shrunken liver edge and a palpable spleen tip 2 cm below the left costal margin.
No shifting dullness to percussion and fluid wave test is negative.
Digital rectal examination reveals copious black, tarry, sticky stool on the glove with no palpable rectal masses.
